1. Spectrum of a bounded operator

For a bounded operator $T$ on a Hilbert space $H$, the spectrum is $$\sigma(T) = \{\lambda \in \mathbb{C} : T-\lambda I \text{ is not invertible in } B(H)\}.$$ On finite-dimensional $H$ this is just the set of eigenvalues. In infinite dimensions $T-\lambda I$ can fail to be invertible in three different ways, and the spectrum decomposes accordingly:

  • Point spectrum $\sigma_p(T)$: $T-\lambda I$ has non-trivial kernel — $\lambda$ is a genuine eigenvalue.
  • Continuous spectrum $\sigma_c(T)$: $T-\lambda I$ is injective and its range is dense but not closed.
  • Residual spectrum $\sigma_r(T)$: $T-\lambda I$ is injective but its range is not dense.

Three theorems anchor the picture: $\sigma(T)$ is a non-empty compact subset of $\overline{B(0,\|T\|)}\subset\mathbb{C}$ (Liouville for the resolvent), and the spectral radius formula $r(T)=\lim_n \|T^n\|^{1/n}$ recovers it from the norm.

2. Self-adjoint spectrum lives on $\mathbb{R}$

If $T = T^*$ on a Hilbert space, two strong constraints follow:

  • $\sigma(T) \subset \mathbb{R}$. The proof: for $\lambda = a + ib$ with $b \ne 0$, $\|(T-\lambda)\varphi\|^2 = \|(T-a)\varphi\|^2 + b^2\|\varphi\|^2 \ge b^2\|\varphi\|^2$, so $T-\lambda$ is bounded below — and the same inequality for $T-\bar\lambda = (T-\lambda)^*$ shows the range is dense, giving invertibility.
  • $r(T) = \|T\|$. Because $\|T^2\| = \|T^*T\| = \|T\|^2$ for self-adjoint $T$, induction gives $\|T^{2^k}\| = \|T\|^{2^k}$, and the spectral-radius limit equals $\|T\|$.

The residual spectrum is also empty: if $T-\lambda$ has range not dense for $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $\overline{\mathrm{Ran}(T-\lambda)}^{\perp}=\ker(T-\lambda)^*=\ker(T-\lambda)\ne 0$, so $\lambda$ is actually an eigenvalue — contradiction. Self-adjoint spectra split into point + continuous parts only.

(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById("herm-svg");

  const cx = 320, cy = 110, sx = 80;
  function clear(){ while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild); }
  function randHerm(n){
    // build A = (B + B*)/2 with B real-complex Gaussian
    const A = [];
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){ A.push(new Array(n)); }
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
      for(let j=i;j<n;j++){
        const re = (Math.random()*2 - 1) * 1.2;
        const im = i===j ? 0 : (Math.random()*2 - 1) * 1.2;
        A[i][j] = [re, im];
        A[j][i] = [re, -im];
      }
    }
    return A;
  }
  // Power iteration with deflation for n=4 small Hermitian — cheap eigenvalue extraction.
  // For demo purposes: convert to real symmetric 2n x 2n form and use Jacobi.
  function eigsHerm(A){
    const n = A.length;
    // expand to real 2n × 2n: [[Re, -Im], [Im, Re]]
    const N = 2*n;
    const M = [];
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){ M.push(new Array(N).fill(0)); }
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
      for(let j=0;j<n;j++){
        const [re, im] = A[i][j];
        M[i][j] = re;
        M[i+n][j+n] = re;
        M[i][j+n] = -im;
        M[i+n][j] = im;
      }
    }
    // Jacobi eigenvalue (symmetric)
    const eps = 1e-10;
    let maxIter = 200;
    while(maxIter--){
      let p=0, q=1, big=0;
      for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
        for(let j=i+1;j<N;j++){
          if(Math.abs(M[i][j]) > big){ big = Math.abs(M[i][j]); p=i; q=j; }
        }
      }
      if(big < eps) break;
      const theta = (M[q][q]-M[p][p])/(2*M[p][q]);
      const t = Math.sign(theta)/(Math.abs(theta)+Math.sqrt(1+theta*theta));
      const c = 1/Math.sqrt(1+t*t), s = t*c;
      const Mpp = M[p][p], Mqq = M[q][q], Mpq = M[p][q];
      M[p][p] = c*c*Mpp - 2*s*c*Mpq + s*s*Mqq;
      M[q][q] = s*s*Mpp + 2*s*c*Mpq + c*c*Mqq;
      M[p][q] = M[q][p] = 0;
      for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
        if(i!==p && i!==q){
          const Mip = M[i][p], Miq = M[i][q];
          M[i][p] = M[p][i] = c*Mip - s*Miq;
          M[i][q] = M[q][i] = s*Mip + c*Miq;
        }
      }
    }
    // each Hermitian eigenvalue appears twice in M; collect distinct
    const evs = [];
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++) evs.push(M[i][i]);
    evs.sort((a,b)=>a-b);
    const uniq = [];
    for(let i=0;i<evs.length;i+=2) uniq.push((evs[i]+evs[i+1])/2);
    return uniq;
  }

    // real axis

3. Spectral theorem (compact self-adjoint)

The cleanest spectral statement: a compact self-adjoint operator $K$ on a separable Hilbert space admits an orthonormal basis $(\varphi_n)$ of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues $\lambda_n \to 0$. Concretely: $$K = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \lambda_n \langle \varphi_n, \cdot\rangle\, \varphi_n.$$ Each non-zero eigenvalue has a finite-dimensional eigenspace (compactness rules out infinite-dimensional ones). The kernel of $K$ may still be infinite-dimensional.

The canonical example: the Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator $(Kf)(x)=\int_0^1 k(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ with $k\in L^2([0,1]^2)$ symmetric ($k(x,y)=k(y,x)$). It produces a compact self-adjoint $K$, and the eigenfunction expansion is the Mercer-type series for $k$.

4. Spectral theorem (bounded self-adjoint)

When the spectrum is no longer discrete, summation $\sum \lambda_n P_n$ must be replaced by integration. The bounded spectral theorem produces a unique projection-valued measure (PVM) $E$ on the Borel sets of $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb{R}$ such that $$T = \int_{\sigma(T)} \lambda\, dE_\lambda, \qquad f(T) = \int_{\sigma(T)} f(\lambda)\, dE_\lambda \text{ for } f\in C(\sigma(T)).$$ $E_\Omega$ is an orthogonal projection for every Borel $\Omega$, and $E_\Omega E_{\Omega'} = E_{\Omega\cap\Omega'}$. The map $f\mapsto f(T)$ is an isometric *-homomorphism $C(\sigma(T)) \to C^*(T,1)$ — Gelfand–Naimark applied to a single self-adjoint generator.

Equivalent formulations: every bounded self-adjoint operator is unitarily equivalent to a multiplication operator $M_g\colon L^2(X,\mu)\to L^2(X,\mu)$ for some bounded measurable $g$ on a measure space $(X,\mu)$.

5. Unbounded operators and Stone's theorem

The most important operators in physics are unbounded: position $X$, momentum $P=-i\partial_x$, the Laplacian $-\Delta$, the harmonic-oscillator Hamiltonian. They cannot be elements of $B(H)$, so the bounded spectral theorem does not directly apply. The fix: work with densely defined closed operators on a domain $\mathrm{Dom}(T)\subset H$.

An operator is symmetric if $\langle T\varphi,\psi\rangle = \langle\varphi, T\psi\rangle$ for $\varphi,\psi\in\mathrm{Dom}(T)$, and self-adjoint if additionally $\mathrm{Dom}(T) = \mathrm{Dom}(T^*)$. The two conditions diverge once you leave bounded operators: symmetric is too weak. Self-adjoint operators admit a spectral resolution $T = \int_\mathbb{R} \lambda\, dE_\lambda$ on their natural domain.

Stone's theorem upgrades this to dynamics: strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups $\{U(t)\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ are in bijection with self-adjoint operators $A$ via $U(t)=e^{itA}$, with $A\varphi = -i\,\frac{d}{dt}U(t)\varphi|_{t=0}$ on the natural domain. Quantum dynamics, heat flow, and wave propagation are all instances.

6. Compact operators and the Fredholm alternative

Compactness is the analytic upgrade of "finite-dimensional behaviour." An operator $K\in B(H)$ is compact if it sends bounded sets to precompact sets — equivalently, if $K$ is the norm-limit of finite-rank operators. The compacts $\mathcal{K}(H)$ form a closed two-sided $*$-ideal of $B(H)$.

The miracle, due to Riesz, Schauder, and Fredholm, is that for $\lambda\ne 0$ the operator $T-\lambda I$ with $T=K$ behaves like a square matrix:

Fredholm alternative. Let $K\in\mathcal{K}(H)$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$. Then $K-\lambda I$ is Fredholm of index $0$:
  • $\dim\ker(K-\lambda I) = \dim\mathrm{coker}(K-\lambda I) < \infty$.
  • $\mathrm{Ran}(K-\lambda I)$ is closed.
  • The equation $Kx-\lambda x = y$ is solvable iff $y\perp\ker(K^*-\bar\lambda I)$.
  • Either $K-\lambda I$ is invertible, or $\lambda\in\sigma_p(K)$ with finite-dimensional eigenspace — never anything in between.

The non-zero spectrum is therefore discrete, with finite multiplicities and accumulating only at $0$ — exactly the picture from the compact spectral theorem, now without self-adjointness. The general index of a Fredholm operator $T$ is $\operatorname{ind}(T)=\dim\ker T - \dim\mathrm{coker} T\in\mathbb{Z}$, a homotopy invariant under norm-continuous deformations through Fredholm operators. For $K-\lambda I$ above, $\operatorname{ind}=0$ because $K\mapsto 0$ is a path of compact perturbations and $-\lambda I$ is invertible.

The classical model: integral equations $\varphi(x) - \lambda\int_0^1 k(x,y)\varphi(y)\,dy = f(x)$ with $L^2$ kernel. The compact operator $K\varphi(x)=\int k(x,y)\varphi(y)\,dy$ controls the equation; for $\lambda^{-1}\notin\sigma(K)$ there is a unique solution, otherwise the equation is solvable iff $f$ is orthogonal to all solutions of the homogeneous adjoint equation. Fredholm's 1903 paper invented this game — and it underlies modern elliptic-PDE theory and index theory.

7. Trace-class and Hilbert–Schmidt: the Schatten ideals

Compact operators come with a finer filtration. Every compact $T\in\mathcal{K}(H)$ has singular values $s_n(T)$, the eigenvalues of $|T|=\sqrt{T^*T}$ in non-increasing order. The Schatten $p$-ideal is

$$\mathcal{S}_p(H) \;=\; \Big\{T\in\mathcal{K}(H) : \|T\|_p^p := \sum_{n}s_n(T)^p < \infty\Big\},\qquad p\in[1,\infty).$$

The two cases that name themselves:

  • $\mathcal{S}_2$, the Hilbert–Schmidt operators. The norm $\|T\|_{HS}^2 = \sum\|Te_n\|^2 = \sum s_n(T)^2$ is independent of the orthonormal basis $(e_n)$, and $\mathcal{S}_2$ itself is a Hilbert space with inner product $\langle T,S\rangle_{HS}=\operatorname{tr}(S^*T)$. On $L^2(X,\mu)$, an integral operator $K_kf(x)=\int k(x,y)f(y)\,d\mu(y)$ is HS iff $k\in L^2(X\times X,\mu\otimes\mu)$, with $\|K_k\|_{HS}=\|k\|_2$.
  • $\mathcal{S}_1$, the trace-class operators. The functional $\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_n\langle Te_n,e_n\rangle$ converges absolutely on $\mathcal{S}_1$ and is independent of the ONB; it is positive on positive operators and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ when at least one factor is trace-class. For positive $T$, $\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum s_n(T)$ — finiteness defines the ideal.

The chain of inclusions matches summability:

$$\text{finite-rank}\;\subset\;\mathcal{S}_1\;\subset\;\mathcal{S}_2\;\subset\;\mathcal{S}_p\;\subset\;\mathcal{K}(H)\;\subset\;B(H),\qquad 1\le p\le\infty.$$

Hölder for Schatten norms: if $1/p+1/q=1/r$ then $\|TS\|_r\le\|T\|_p\|S\|_q$. The case $p=q=2$, $r=1$ is most useful: the product of two HS operators is trace-class.

Schatten duality. Pairing by $\langle T,S\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(TS)$ identifies

$$\mathcal{K}(H)^*\cong\mathcal{S}_1, \qquad \mathcal{S}_1^*\cong B(H), \qquad \mathcal{S}_p^*\cong\mathcal{S}_q\;(1So $\mathcal{S}_1$ is the unique predual of $B(H)$: a normal state on $B(H)$ is the same as a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ — the density matrix of quantum statistical mechanics.

8. Weyl's law: hearing the volume of a drum

For the Dirichlet Laplacian $-\Delta$ on a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, the spectrum is a discrete sequence $0 < \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty$ of eigenvalues with finite multiplicity (compact resolvent). The eigenvalue counting function is

$$N(\lambda) \;=\; \#\{n : \lambda_n \le \lambda\}.$$

Hermann Weyl proved in 1911 that, as $\lambda\to\infty$,

$$\boxed{\;N(\lambda) \;\sim\; \frac{\omega_d\,|\Omega|}{(2\pi)^d}\,\lambda^{d/2}\;}\qquad(\omega_d = \text{volume of unit ball in }\mathbb{R}^d).$$

Equivalently $\lambda_n\sim C_d\,(n/|\Omega|)^{2/d}$. The leading-order asymptotics of the spectrum recover two geometric invariants:

  • The dimension $d$ — through the exponent $d/2$.
  • The volume $|\Omega|$ — through the prefactor.

The proof, in modern dress: a semiclassical argument. The trace of the heat kernel $e^{t\Delta}$ on $\Omega$ has the small-$t$ expansion

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl(e^{t\Delta}\bigr) = \sum_n e^{-\lambda_n t} \sim \frac{|\Omega|}{(4\pi t)^{d/2}} - \frac{|\partial\Omega|}{4\,(4\pi t)^{(d-1)/2}} + O(t^{-(d-2)/2})\quad(t\to 0^+),$$

and a Tauberian theorem (Karamata) inverts this to Weyl's law. The second coefficient gives the boundary length — Pleijel showed that you also hear the perimeter; the third gives the Euler characteristic. So you hear: $d$, $|\Omega|$, $|\partial\Omega|$, $\chi(\Omega)$.

Can you hear the shape of a drum? Mark Kac asked in 1966 whether $\sigma(-\Delta)$ determines $\Omega$ up to isometry. The answer is no: Gordon, Webb & Wolpert (1992) constructed isospectral non-isometric polygonal domains. But you can hear $d$, $|\Omega|$, $|\partial\Omega|$, and the topology — Weyl, Pleijel, Kac.

The same machinery extends to compact Riemannian manifolds (Minakshisundaram–Pleijel) and to elliptic pseudodifferential operators (Hörmander) — a corner of analysis where spectrum, geometry, and heat propagation are one story.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById("wl-svg");
  const out = document.getElementById("wl-readout");
  const stat = document.getElementById("wl-stat");
  const sa = document.getElementById("wl-a"), sb = document.getElementById("wl-b"), sl = document.getElementById("wl-l");
  const left=60, right=620, top=20, bot=240;
  function clear(){ while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild); }
  function exactCount(a, b, lam){
    // # (m,n) ∈ Z_{≥1}² with π² (m²/a² + n²/b²) ≤ λ
    // ⇔ m²/a² + n²/b² ≤ λ/π²
    const R = lam/(Math.PI*Math.PI);
    const Mmax = Math.floor(a*Math.sqrt(R));
    let count = 0;
    for(let m=1; m<=Mmax; m++){
      const rem = R - m*m/(a*a);
      if(rem <= 0) continue;
      const Nmax = Math.floor(b*Math.sqrt(rem));
      count += Nmax;
    }
    return count;
  }
  function draw(){
    clear();
    const a = +sa.value/10;     // 0.5 .. 2.0
    const b = +sb.value/10;
    const lamMax = +sl.value;
    // sample N(λ) on a grid 0..lamMax (step ~ lamMax/200), exact and Weyl
    const M = 200;
    const exact = [], weyl = [];
    for(let i=0;i<=M;i++){
      const lam = (i/M) * lamMax;
      exact.push(exactCount(a,b,lam));
      weyl.push(a*b*lam/(4*Math.PI));
    }
    const Nmax = Math.max(exact[exact.length-1], weyl[weyl.length-1], 1);
    const xMap = (lam)=>left + (right-left)*(lam/lamMax);
    const yMap = (n)=>bot - (bot-top-20)*(n/Nmax);
    // axes
    svg.appendChild(SVG("line",{x1:left,y1:bot,x2:right,y2:bot,stroke:"var(--line)"}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG("line",{x1:left,y1:top,x2:left,y2:bot,stroke:"var(--line)"}));
    const xl = SVG("text",{x:right-6,y:bot+18,"font-size":11,fill:"var(--mute)","text-anchor":"end"}); xl.textContent="λ"; svg.appendChild(xl);
    const yl = SVG("text",{x:left-10,y:top+12,"font-size":11,fill:"var(--mute)","text-anchor":"end"}); yl.textContent="N(λ)"; svg.appendChild(yl);
    // exact step plot
    let dE = `M ${xMap(0)} ${yMap(0)}`;
    for(let i=1;i<=M;i++){
      const lam = (i/M)*lamMax;
      dE += ` L ${xMap(lam)} ${yMap(exact[i-1])} L ${xMap(lam)} ${yMap(exact[i])}`;
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG("path",{d:dE, fill:"none", stroke:"var(--cyan)", "stroke-width":1.4}));
    // Weyl line
    const dW = `M ${xMap(0)} ${yMap(weyl[0])} L ${xMap(lamMax)} ${yMap(weyl[M])}`;
    svg.appendChild(SVG("path",{d:dW, fill:"none", stroke:"var(--yellow)", "stroke-width":2.2, "stroke-dasharray":"6 4"}));
    // legend
    svg.appendChild(SVG("line",{x1:right-220,y1:top+10,x2:right-200,y2:top+10,stroke:"var(--cyan)","stroke-width":1.4}));
    const l1 = SVG("text",{x:right-194,y:top+14,"font-size":12,fill:"var(--cyan)"}); l1.textContent="exact lattice count"; svg.appendChild(l1);
    svg.appendChild(SVG("line",{x1:right-220,y1:top+30,x2:right-200,y2:top+30,stroke:"var(--yellow)","stroke-width":2.2,"stroke-dasharray":"6 4"}));
    const l2 = SVG("text",{x:right-194,y:top+34,"font-size":12,fill:"var(--yellow)"}); l2.textContent="Weyl: |Ω|λ/(4π)"; svg.appendChild(l2);
    // stat
    const Ne = exactCount(a,b,lamMax);
    const Nw = a*b*lamMax/(4*Math.PI);
    const ratio = Ne/Math.max(Nw,1);
    stat.textContent = `a=${a.toFixed(1)}, b=${b.toFixed(1)}, λ=${lamMax}: N=${Ne}, Weyl≈${Nw.toFixed(1)}, ratio=${ratio.toFixed(3)}`;
    out.textContent = `Dirichlet eigenvalues on [0,${a.toFixed(1)}]×[0,${b.toFixed(1)}]: λ_{m,n} = π²(m²/a² + n²/b²), m,n ≥ 1.\nN(λ) counts lattice points (m,n) ∈ Z_{≥1}² in the quarter-ellipse m²/a² + n²/b² ≤ λ/π².\nWeyl's law: N(λ) ~ |Ω|λ/(4π) = ab λ/(4π) as λ → ∞.\nThe boundary correction is -|∂Ω|√λ/(4π) = -(2a+2b)√λ/(4π) ≈ ${(-(2*a+2*b)*Math.sqrt(lamMax)/(4*Math.PI)).toFixed(1)}, accounting for most of the gap to the leading term.`;
  }
  [sa, sb, sl].forEach(s=>s.addEventListener("input", draw));
  draw();
})();
</script>

9. Applications: quantum mechanics, PDE, harmonic analysis

Spectral theory's reach is wide:

  • Quantum mechanics. Observables are self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space; their spectra are the possible measured values, and the spectral measure is the Born rule. Hamiltonians generate unitary time evolution $U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$.
  • PDE. Elliptic operators (Laplacian, Schrödinger) on bounded domains have compact resolvent; eigenfunctions diagonalize the heat and wave semigroups. On unbounded domains, the continuous spectrum carries scattering states.
  • Harmonic analysis. Translation-invariant operators on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ are diagonalized by the Fourier transform: $\widehat{Tf}(\xi) = m(\xi)\hat f(\xi)$, the symbol $m$ being the spectral multiplier. Pontryagin duality generalizes this to all locally compact abelian groups.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById("osc-svg");
  const out = document.getElementById("osc-readout");
  const stat = document.getElementById("osc-stat");
  const sw = document.getElementById("osc-w");
  const sN = document.getElementById("osc-N");
  const left=60, right=600, top=20, bot=290;
  const cx = (left+right)/2;
  function clear(){ while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild); }
  function draw(){
    clear();
    const wRaw = +sw.value/10;        // ω in display units
    const N = +sN.value;
    // energy axis: y-up
    const Emax = (N - 0.5) * wRaw + 0.4;
    const yE = (E)=>bot - (bot-top-10) * (E/Emax);
    const xq = (q)=>cx + 32 * q;       // position
    // axes
    svg.appendChild(SVG("line",{x1:left,y1:bot,x2:right,y2:bot,stroke:"var(--line)"}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG("line",{x1:cx,y1:top,x2:cx,y2:bot,stroke:"var(--line)"}));
    const xl = SVG("text",{x:right-10,y:bot+18,"font-size":11,fill:"var(--mute)"}); xl.textContent="x"; svg.appendChild(xl);
    const yl = SVG("text",{x:cx+8,y:top+12,"font-size":11,fill:"var(--mute)"}); yl.textContent="E"; svg.appendChild(yl);
    // potential V(x) = 0.5 ω² x²  (display scaled)
    const pts = [];
    for(let i=-100;i<=100;i++){
      const q = i/14;
      const E = 0.5 * wRaw*wRaw * q*q;
      if(E > Emax) continue;
      pts.push([xq(q), yE(E)]);
    }
    if(pts.length){
      const d = pts.map((p,i)=>(i?"L":"M")+p[0]+","+p[1]).join(" ");
      svg.appendChild(SVG("path",{d, fill:"none", stroke:"var(--violet)","stroke-width":2}));
    }
    // energy levels
    for(let n=0;n<N;n++){
      const E = (n + 0.5) * wRaw;
      // classical turning points: 0.5 ω² q² = E ⇒ q = √(2E)/ω
      const q = Math.sqrt(2*E)/wRaw;
      const x1 = xq(-q), x2 = xq(q), yy = yE(E);
      svg.appendChild(SVG("line",{x1, y1:yy, x2, y2:yy, stroke:"var(--cyan)","stroke-width":2}));
      const lab = SVG("text",{x:right-6,y:yy+4,"font-size":11,fill:"var(--cyan)","text-anchor":"end"});
      lab.textContent = `E_${n} = ${(n+0.5).toFixed(1)} ℏω`;
      svg.appendChild(lab);
    }
    // ground-state badge
    const tg = SVG("text",{x:left+6,y:yE(0.5*wRaw)-6,"font-size":11,fill:"var(--yellow)"});
    tg.textContent = "ground state E_0 = ½ℏω";
    svg.appendChild(tg);
    // potential label
    const tp = SVG("text",{x:left+6,y:bot-10,"font-size":11,fill:"var(--violet)"});
    tp.textContent = `V(x) = ½mω²x²`;
    svg.appendChild(tp);
    stat.textContent = `ω = ${wRaw.toFixed(1)},  N levels = ${N},  spacing ℏω = ${wRaw.toFixed(2)}`;
    out.textContent = `H = -ℏ²/(2m) ∂²/∂x² + ½ m ω² x².  Discrete spectrum E_n = (n + ½)ℏω, n = 0, 1, 2, ...  Ladder operators a, a* shift between levels: H = ℏω(a*a + ½).  Eigenfunctions = Hermite polynomials × Gaussian.`;
  }
  sw.addEventListener("input", draw);
  sN.addEventListener("input", draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>
